title: Alcohols: Classification, Preparation, Reactions and Uses
summary: The structure and classification of alcohols, their properties, preparation by fermentation and hydration, and their reactions and uses.

p: Alcohols are derivatives of alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by a hydroxyl group (–OH). General formula for simple alcohols: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH.
By the number of –OH groups: monohydric (one: ethanol CH₃CH₂OH); dihydric (two: ethane-1,2-diol, glycol); trihydric (three: propane-1,2,3-triol, glycerol); polyhydric (many: sugars such as glucose).

By the carbon carrying the –OH: primary (1°): attached to a carbon bonded to one other carbon (CH₃CH₂OH); secondary (2°): attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbons (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, propan-2-ol); tertiary (3°): attached to a carbon bonded to three other carbons ((CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol).

Boiling points are higher than those of alkanes of similar size, because of hydrogen bonding between molecules. The lower alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propanol) dissolve in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water; solubility falls as the molecules get larger. They have a characteristic smell and are poor conductors.

1. Fermentation of carbohydrates: glucose is changed by the enzyme zymase in yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (at about 35 °C, without air). This is how palm wine, beer and industrial ethanol from molasses are made.
2. Hydration of ethene: C₂H₄ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅OH, with phosphoric acid on a support as catalyst, at about 300 °C and 60 to 70 atm.
3. Reduction of aldehydes and ketones: an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol and a ketone gives a secondary alcohol.
1. Combustion: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (clean flame).
2. With sodium: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂ (sodium ethoxide; hydrogen is given off).

3. Oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange to green): a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid (CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO → CH₃COOH); a secondary alcohol gives a ketone (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃COCH₃); a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised easily.
4. Esterification: with a carboxylic acid and concentrated H₂SO₄: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
5. Dehydration: with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C ethanol gives ethene: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O.

Ethanol: drinks, solvent, antiseptic, motor fuel (blended with petrol), making esters, perfumes and medicines. Methanol: making methanal (formaldehyde), solvent, antifreeze and fuel (methanol is very poisonous and can cause blindness). Glycerol: cosmetics, explosives (nitroglycerine) and food. Ethylene glycol: antifreeze and polyester.

title: Ethers and Phenols, and Comparison with Alcohols
summary: The structure, preparation, reactions and uses of ethers and phenols, and a comparison of alcohols, ethers and phenols.

p: Ethers have two alkyl or aryl groups joined to the same oxygen atom: R–O–R′. Examples: diethyl ether C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ (symmetrical) and methyl ethyl ether CH₃–O–C₂H₅ (unsymmetrical).

Physical properties: volatile and highly flammable; slightly soluble in water; boiling points much lower than alcohols of the same molar mass, because ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other. They are more volatile than the alcohols for this reason.

Preparation: (1) dehydration of an alcohol with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. (2) Williamson synthesis: sodium alkoxide with an alkyl halide: C₂H₅ONa + CH₃I → CH₃OC₂H₅ + NaI.
Reactions: burn to give CO₂ and H₂O; react with hot concentrated HI: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅I + C₂H₅OH; and form explosive peroxides when kept in air.
Uses: diethyl ether as an anaesthetic (less used now because it is flammable), solvents in laboratories and industry, and starting materials for plastics, perfumes and drugs.
Phenols have an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring. The simplest is phenol, C₆H₅OH. It is a colourless solid with a characteristic smell, fairly soluble in water, and weakly acidic.

Preparation: (1) fusing sodium benzenesulphonate with NaOH: C₆H₅SO₃Na + 2NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + Na₂SO₃ + H₂O, then acidifying: C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl. (2) Hydrolysing chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure.

Reactions: with sodium (hydrogen is given off); with NaOH to give sodium phenoxide and water, C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O (ethanol does not react with NaOH); with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr; with dilute nitric acid to give nitrophenols. Test: neutral iron(III) chloride gives a violet colour.
Uses: antiseptics and disinfectants; making aspirin and other drugs; making plastics (Bakelite), dyes and explosives.

sections.h: Why phenol is more acidic than ethanol
p: When phenol loses H⁺, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion is spread (delocalised) into the benzene ring, which makes the ion stable. In the ethoxide ion the charge stays on the oxygen and is less stable. So phenol gives up H⁺ more readily and reacts with NaOH, but ethanol does not.

title: Aldehydes and Ketones: Structure and Preparation
summary: The carbonyl group, general formulae and examples of aldehydes and ketones, and their preparation.

p: Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the group is polar: the carbon is slightly positive and attracts nucleophiles. Aldehydes: R–CHO, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen (methanal HCHO, ethanal CH₃CHO, benzaldehyde C₆H₅CHO). Ketones: R–CO–R′, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups (propanone CH₃COCH₃, butanone CH₃COC₂H₅).
1. Oxidation of a primary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling off the aldehyde as it forms (so that it is not oxidised further): CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O.

2. Methanal from methanol: air and a hot silver (or copper) catalyst: CH₃OH + ½O₂ → HCHO + H₂O. Methanal is also made by the oxidation of methane over molybdenum or copper catalysts: CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O.
3. Hydroformylation (oxo process): alkene + CO + H₂ with a cobalt or rhodium catalyst: CH₂=CH₂ + CO + H₂ → CH₃CH₂CHO (propanal).
1. Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O.
2. Friedel-Crafts acylation (aromatic ketones): C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl, with AlCl₃ as catalyst.
3. Heating the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid: (CH₃COO)₂Ca → CH₃COCH₃ + CaCO₃.
4. Hydration of an alkyne (water, dilute H₂SO₄ and Hg²⁺): propyne gives propanone (Markovnikov's rule: the –OH goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens). (Ethyne itself gives an aldehyde, ethanal.)
Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (with strong oxidation). Secondary alcohol → ketone (which resists further oxidation). Tertiary alcohols are resistant.

title: Identification Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones
summary: The 2,4-DNP, Tollens', Fehling's, Benedict's and Schiff's tests, a comparison of aldehydes and ketones, and their uses.

sections.h: General test for the carbonyl group
p: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP): both aldehydes and ketones give a yellow-orange crystalline precipitate (a hydrazone). This shows a carbonyl group is present.
Tollens' test (ammoniacal silver nitrate), warmed: aldehydes give a silver mirror. RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O. Ketones give no reaction.

Fehling's test (Fehling's solution A and B, warmed): aldehydes reduce the deep blue Cu²⁺ complex to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O. Ketones do not react. (Benzaldehyde, which is aromatic, does not give a positive Fehling's test.)
Benedict's test: like Fehling's: a red precipitate with aldehydes (aliphatic).
Schiff's test: aldehydes restore the pink or magenta colour of Schiff's reagent. Ketones do not.

img.alt: A decision tree for carbonyl compound tests using 2,4-DNP, Tollens' test and Fehling's test

sections.h: Why aldehydes are oxidised but ketones are not
p: An aldehyde has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so it can easily be oxidised to a carboxylic acid (this is what reduces the silver or copper ions). A ketone has no such hydrogen, so it is resistant to mild oxidation.

title: Carboxylic Acids: Structure, Properties and Reactions
summary: The carboxyl group, naming, physical properties, acidity and reactions of carboxylic acids, and their uses.

p: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH (a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon). General formula RCOOH. Examples: methanoic acid HCOOH (formic acid, from ants), ethanoic acid CH₃COOH (acetic acid, in vinegar) and benzoic acid C₆H₅COOH. IUPAC name: change the –e of the alkane to –oic acid.

The lower members (methanoic and ethanoic acids) are colourless liquids with a sharp smell; higher members are solids. Boiling points are higher than those of alcohols of similar size, because acid molecules form pairs (dimers) joined by two hydrogen bonds. Small acids dissolve in water; solubility falls as the chain gets longer. They taste sour and are corrosive when concentrated.

Carboxylic acids are weak acids, partly ionised in water: RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺. They turn blue litmus red. They are stronger acids than alcohols, because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance (the negative charge is shared by the two oxygen atoms).
1. With bases: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
2. With carbonates: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ (effervescence of CO₂ is a test for an acid).
3. With reactive metals: 2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COONa + H₂.
4. Esterification with an alcohol and concentrated H₂SO₄: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O.
5. Reduction with LiAlH₄ gives a primary alcohol.
Oxidation of a primary alcohol: CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heating under reflux). Oxidation of an aldehyde: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH.

Ethanoic acid (vinegar): food and preserving, solvent, making esters. Methanoic acid: tanning leather, dyeing cloth and preserving silage. Benzoic acid: a preservative in soft drinks and juices. Dicarboxylic acids: raw materials for nylon and polyester.

title: Esters: Structure, Preparation, Hydrolysis and Uses
summary: The structure and naming of esters, esterification, acid and alkaline hydrolysis, and the uses of esters.

p: An ester is formed when the hydrogen of the –COOH group of a carboxylic acid is replaced by an alkyl group: R–COOR′. Naming: alkyl alkanoate, with the alkyl part from the alcohol and the alkanoate from the acid. CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate; CH₃COOC₂H₅ is ethyl ethanoate; C₂H₅COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate.

A carboxylic acid and an alcohol, heated with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid (a catalyst and also a dehydrating agent), form an ester and water: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O. The reaction is reversible. In the mechanism, the acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, the alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon, a proton moves and water is lost. The acid supplies the –OH that is lost with the H of the alcohol.

img.alt: The reversible esterification reaction of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with sulphuric acid as catalyst to give an ester and water

p: Propanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl propanoate. Methanoic acid + propan-1-ol → propyl methanoate. Benzoic acid + methanol → methyl benzoate.

Esters have pleasant fruity smells. The smaller esters are liquids and the larger are waxy solids. They do not dissolve in water. Their boiling points are lower than those of acids of the same molar mass, because there are no hydrogen bonds between ester molecules.

Acid hydrolysis (reversible): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH (dilute acid catalyst). Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification, not reversible): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH. This is how soap is made from fats and oils (esters of glycerol). Esters burn with a clean flame to CO₂ and H₂O.

Perfumes and flavours (isoamyl ethanoate smells of bananas; ethyl butanoate of pineapple); solvents for paints and varnishes (ethyl ethanoate); making plastics and synthetic fibres (polyesters such as Terylene); soap making; plasticisers in PVC.

title: Polymers and Plastics: Types and Uses
summary: Monomers and polymers, natural and synthetic polymers, addition and condensation polymerisation, thermoplastics and thermosets, and the uses of common plastics.

p: Poly means many and meros means parts. A polymer is a very large molecule (a macromolecule) made of many repeating small units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds. The reaction is polymerisation. The number of repeating units in a chain is the degree of polymerisation. Molar masses can reach millions. Examples: ethene → polyethene; glucose → starch and cellulose; isoprene → natural rubber; amino acids → proteins.

img.alt: A chart classifying polymers into natural polymers (DNA, protein, rubber) and synthetic polymers (addition polymers like polyethene and condensation polymers like nylon)

p: Natural polymers: starch, cellulose and glycogen (from glucose); proteins (from amino acids); DNA and RNA (from nucleotides); natural rubber (polyisoprene). Synthetic polymers: polyethene, polystyrene, PVC, nylon, Terylene, Bakelite and silicone rubbers.

Unsaturated monomers (with C=C) join without losing any small molecule (heat, pressure and a catalyst are needed). nCH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ polyethene. PVC from chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl); polystyrene from styrene (C₆H₅CH=CH₂); Teflon (PTFE) from tetrafluoroethene (CF₂=CF₂): nCF₂=CF₂ → (–CF₂–CF₂–)ₙ.

Monomers with two functional groups join, and a small molecule such as water or HCl is lost each time. Nylon-6,6: hexane-1,6-diamine H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + hexanedioic (adipic) acid HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO]ₙ– + H₂O (an amide, or peptide, link). Terylene (polyester): ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) → –[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ– + H₂O. Bakelite: phenol + methanal.

img.alt: The repeating units of polyethene, polypropene, PVC, polystyrene, Terylene and a polyurethane

p: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be re-moulded: they have long chains with no cross-links (polyethene, PVC, polystyrene). Thermosetting plastics harden permanently when heated and cannot be re-moulded: they have many cross-links between chains (Bakelite, melamine, epoxy resins). By mechanical properties: elastomers are stretchy (natural rubber, neoprene), fibres are strong threads (nylon, Terylene, silk) and plastics are rigid or flexible solids.

Polyethene: bags, films, bottles, buckets and pipes. PVC: wire insulation, water pipes, floor tiles and roofing. Polystyrene: disposable cups, packaging foam, insulation. Teflon: non-stick pans and gaskets. Nylon: clothes, ropes, nets, toothbrush bristles and parachutes. Terylene: clothes, curtains and conveyor belts. Bakelite: electric switches and plugs, handles of pans. Rubber: tyres, shoes and shock absorbers. PVC is good for cable insulation because it does not conduct and it is flexible and cheap; Bakelite is used for switches because it does not soften when heated.

title: Dangers of Plastics and How to Control Them
summary: The harm done by plastics to the environment and health, and recycling, biodegradable alternatives and other solutions.

p: 1. Non-biodegradable: plastics stay in soil and water for decades. They block drains and cause flooding and ugly rubbish heaps.
2. Poisonous when burnt: burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride; incomplete burning of plastics gives carbon monoxide and dioxins, which can cause cancer.
3. Marine pollution: fish, turtles and birds swallow plastic and die. Tiny pieces (microplastics) enter the food chain and reach humans.
4. Health hazards: plastic packaging can release additives such as phthalates and BPA into food and drinks, which can disturb hormones.
5. Resource use: most plastics are made from petroleum, which is running out.
6. Fire risk: many plastics burn easily and give off dense, poisonous smoke.

Recycling and reuse: collect, melt and re-mould plastics (sort them by type). Biodegradable plastics: made from starch or polylactic acid (PLA), which microbes can break down. Waste management: collect and dispose of waste properly, with laws against dumping. Replacement: use paper, cloth, glass, metal or clay containers. Education: teach people to reduce, reuse and recycle. Laws: ban or tax single-use plastics such as shopping bags and straws.

In many Nigerian cities, plastic sachets and bottles block gutters and make floods worse during the rainy season. Collecting bottles for recycling, using reusable bags and cups, and keeping drains clear are simple things that students can start with.
